newsitem.title: USA: US Republicans to shy from budget economic talks.
newsitem.headline: US Republicans to shy from budget economic talks.

text.p: Republican lawmakers are unlikely to negotiate with the Clinton administration soon over economic assumptions underlying the budget, despite White House pressure to do so, a senior aide said on Tuesday.
"The White House is trying to enter into some type of negotiations," House Budget Committee Staff Director Rick May told the National Association of Manufacturers.
But, he added, "I don't anticipate those negotiations to occur, at least not in the near term."

He said that the Republicans were trying to avoid a public debate on whose economic assumptions are more accurate -- the White House's Office of Management and Budget or the Congressional Budget Office.

May later told reporters that the differences between the two set of economic forecasts might narrow anyway from what they had been previously. "There may be smaller differences than in the past," he said.

The senior Republican aide also said he expects Congress to vote on the balanced budget amendment to the constitution in the first six months of next year. "The balanced budget amendment is coming," he said.
Clinton's Democratic administration opposes the amendement, arguing that it is too rigid, although it supports balancing the budget.
May said the Senate may vote first on the amendement, because the vote in the House looks to be close after the Republicans lost some seats there.
"The preliminary guess is that we are very close in the House," he said, adding, "We don't have much of a margin."
A two-thirds vote in favor by the House and Senate is required for passage of the amendment. It then must be approved three-quarters of the states. Clinton cannot veto the measure.
